\chapter{The Core Verbs}
\label{ch:bn-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I do with six everyday Bengali verbs, pick the ending that matches \bn{তুই}, \bn{তুমি} or \bn{আপনি}, and say why a Bengali verb never changes for gender and why \bn{আছে} has to hand the future to \bn{হবে}.}

Say āmi jāni and āmi tāke chini, separate \bn{জানা} from \bn{চেনা} the way French separates savoir from connaître, hear the vowel harmony that closes chini where chæne stays open, and run the chapter's six verbs back — hôwā, jāwā, āsā, khāwā, dækhā, jānā.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hôwā]{\bn{হওয়া} (hôwā) — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and the be-verb it stands beside}

\label{lesson:BN-C07-howa}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 2 said \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun\textquotedblright{} with no verb at all. Chapter 3 put one back for \textquotedblleft{}how are you.\textquotedblright{} Both were right, and this verb is why.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{হওয়া}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হওয়া}} — \emph{hôwā} — \textbf{to be, to become}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{হই} (\emph{āmi hôi}), \textquotedblleft{}I am, I become.\textquotedblright{} \bn{সে} \bn{হয়} (\emph{se hôy}), \textquotedblleft{}he is.\textquotedblright{} Its future is already in your mouth: \textbf{\bn{হবে}} (\emph{hôbe}) is the \textquotedblleft{}will happen\textquotedblright{} inside Chapter 4's \emph{dækhā hôbe}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{হওয়া}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{ভূ}} (\emph{√bhū}, \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{}) with the \emph{bh-} worn down to a plain \emph{h-}: \emph{bhavati} $\to$ Prakrit \emph{hoï} $\to$ Bengali \emph{hô-}. The root is PIE \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}uH-}, \textquotedblleft{}to grow, to become,\textquotedblright{} and English owns two of its children outright — \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}. Latin built \emph{fuī} (\textquotedblleft{}I was\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{futūrus} on it, which is English \textbf{future}; Greek built \emph{phúsis}, \textquotedblleft{}growth, nature,\textquotedblright{} which is \textbf{physics}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\bn{হ}} is a soft, breathed \emph{h} carrying Bengali's inherent vowel — \emph{hô}, not \emph{ha}. \textbf{\bn{ওয়া}} (\emph{-wā}) is the tail every dictionary-form verb wears; you will meet it again on \bn{খাওয়া} and \bn{যাওয়া}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two be-verbs, and one of them is unfinished}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you mean} & \textbf{what Bengali uses} \\
\midrule
my name is Arun & no verb at all \\
I have a book; it is here & \textbf{\bn{আছে}} (\emph{āchhe}) \\
he will be a teacher & \textbf{\bn{হবে}} (\emph{hôbe}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\bn{আছ}-, the verb behind Chapter 3's \emph{kemon āchho}, means \textbf{being present}. But it is unfinished: it has a present and a past, and nothing else at all. Push it into the future and it stops dead — so Bengali picks up \bn{হ}- (\emph{hôbe}), or Chapter 5's \bn{থাকা} (\emph{āmi thākbo}, \textquotedblleft{}I'll be there\textquotedblright{}). One job, two verbs, split down the middle.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hôwā\textquotedblright{} — be, become — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi hôi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the future you already knew — \textquotedblleft{}hôbe … dækhā hôbe\textquotedblright{}
  \item which verb for \textquotedblleft{}I have a book,\textquotedblright{} and which for \textquotedblleft{}he will be a teacher\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Sanskrit root is \emph{hôwā}, and which two English words are its brothers? (\textbf{√bhū}, \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}.) What can \bn{আছ}- not do? (\textbf{Anything past a present and a past} — it has no future of its own.) So what does Bengali reach for instead? (\textbf{\bn{হবে}}, or \bn{থাকা}.) Next: one verb, three levels of respect.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāwā]{\bn{যাওয়া} (jāwā) — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and the respect that rides on the ending}

\label{lesson:BN-C07-jaowa}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 2 gave you three different words for \textquotedblleft{}you.\textquotedblright{} It did not tell you the rest of the bill: each one bends the verb a different way too.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{যাওয়া}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{যাওয়া}} — \emph{jāwā} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{যাই} (\emph{āmi jāi}), \textquotedblleft{}I go.\textquotedblright{} Same \emph{-i} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} ending as Chapter 5's \emph{bôli}, on the same \emph{-wā} dictionary form you met a moment ago.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{যাওয়া}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{যা}} (\emph{√yā}, \textquotedblleft{}to go, to travel\textquotedblright{}), and the whole northern family walks on it: Hindi \emph{jānā}, Marathi \emph{jāṇe}, Gujarati \emph{javũ}, Punjabi \emph{jāṇā}. Sanskrit's \emph{y-} hardened to a \emph{j-} sound right across eastern Indo-Aryan, which is why Bengali still writes the \emph{y}-letter \textbf{\bn{য}} but says \emph{j}.

Deeper than Sanskrit it goes to PIE \emph{*yeh\textsubscript{2}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to travel\textquotedblright{} — and here is an honest limit: English kept \textbf{no} everyday word from that root. The nearest living cousin is Lithuanian \emph{jóti}, \textquotedblleft{}to ride.\textquotedblright{} A fake English cousin here would be worse than none.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\bn{য}} is the letter Sanskrit reads as \emph{y}; Bengali reads it as \emph{j}, like \textbf{\bn{জ}}. So a written \emph{yā-} is a spoken \emph{jā-} — an un-shift worth keeping, since it disguises dozens of familiar Sanskrit words.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the respect is not in the pronoun, it is in the ending}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who you are speaking to} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}you go\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
\bn{তুই} (\emph{tui}, intimate) & \bn{যাস} (\emph{jāsh}) \\
\bn{তুমি} (\emph{tumi}, familiar) & \bn{যাও} (\emph{jāo}) \\
\bn{আপনি} (\emph{āpni}, respectful) & \bn{যান} (\emph{jān}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three endings, one verb. And the same grading runs on into the third person: \bn{সে} \bn{যায়} (\emph{se jāy}) is \textquotedblleft{}he goes,\textquotedblright{} \bn{তিনি} \bn{যান} (\emph{tini jān}) is \textquotedblleft{}he goes\textquotedblright{} said of someone you respect — the very ending \bn{আপনি} takes. Chapter 5 showed that the ending already means \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} so the pronoun can be dropped. The register cannot. Choose \emph{jāsh} or \emph{jān} and you have placed yourself socially, pronoun or no pronoun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}jāwā\textquotedblright{} — go — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi jāi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ladder — \textquotedblleft{}jāsh … jāo … jān\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two third persons — \textquotedblleft{}se jāy … tini jān\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three \textquotedblleft{}you go\textquotedblright{} forms and who each is for. (\emph{Jāsh} intimate, \emph{jāo} familiar, \emph{jān} respectful.) If you drop the pronoun, is the respect dropped too? (\textbf{No} — it is in the ending, and cannot be dodged.) Does English have a living cousin of this root? (\textbf{No} — Lithuanian \emph{jóti} is as close as it gets.) Next: the verb that asks nothing about who you are.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āsā]{\bn{আসা} (āsā) — \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} the verb that never asks who you are}

\label{lesson:BN-C07-asha}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 1's goodbye, \emph{āshi}, was one form of this verb. Here is the whole of it — and the one question it refuses to ask you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{আসা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আসা}} — \emph{āsā} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{আসি} (\emph{āmi āsi}), \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} — the farewell you already own. \bn{সে} \bn{আসে} (\emph{se āse}), \textquotedblleft{}he comes.\textquotedblright{} \bn{আপনি} \bn{আসেন} (\emph{āpni āsen}), with last lesson's respectful ending.

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{\bn{আ}-} in front is Sanskrit's \emph{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}hither, toward\textquotedblright{} — the very prefix that turns going into coming. Hindi's \emph{ānā} is that \emph{ā-} welded onto \emph{yā-}, the go-verb of the last lesson: \textquotedblleft{}go, but this way.\textquotedblright{} Bengali shows the same prefix on a different stem, and the honest position on that stem is that its history is unsettled; this book will not invent one for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\bn{স}} is written for \emph{s} and spoken, in this word, as \emph{sh} — Bengali's standing \emph{s $\to$ sh} tilt, the same one that makes \emph{namaskāra} into \emph{nômoshkar}. So \bn{আসি} is \emph{āshi}, not \emph{āsi}, though the dictionary form is romanized \emph{āsā}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no gender, not here, not anywhere}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I come,\textquotedblright{} man / woman} \\
\midrule
Hindi & \emph{maiṁ ātā hūṁ} / \emph{maiṁ ātī hūṁ} \\
Marathi & \emph{mī yeto} / \emph{mī yete} \\
Bengali & \emph{āmi āsi} — one form \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Its sisters make you declare your gender to say the plainest thing in the world. Bengali does not. And this is not a shortcut for beginners that the grammar takes back later: \textbf{Bengali has no grammatical gender at all}. Not on verbs, not on nouns, not on adjectives. The past behaves the same way — \bn{আমি} \bn{এলাম} (\emph{āmi elām}), \textquotedblleft{}I came,\textquotedblright{} is one form for everyone, where Gujarati, which hides gender in its present, brings it straight back in \emph{huṁ āvyo} / \emph{huṁ āvī}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āsā\textquotedblright{} — come — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi āshi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the neighbours splitting in two — \textquotedblleft{}ātā … ātī\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yeto … yete\textquotedblright{}
  \item Bengali not splitting — \textquotedblleft{}āmi āsi\textquotedblright{} — and its past, \textquotedblleft{}āmi elām\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \textbf{\bn{আ}-} on this verb mean, and where else have you met it? (\textbf{Hither, toward} — it is the \emph{ā-} inside Hindi's \emph{ānā}.) How many forms of \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} does a Bengali speaker need? (\textbf{One} — \emph{āmi āsi}, whoever is talking.) Is that true of the nouns too? (\textbf{Yes} — Bengali has no grammatical gender anywhere.) Next: a verb that swallows more than food.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khāwā]{\bn{খাওয়া} (khāwā) — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} and the drinking it also does}

\label{lesson:BN-C07-khaowa}



\begin{quote}
Every verb so far has meant roughly what its English gloss means. This one is wider than its gloss, and the extra width is the lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{খাওয়া}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{খাওয়া}} — \emph{khāwā} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{খাই} (\emph{āmi khāi}), \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{} \bn{আপনি} \bn{খান} (\emph{āpni khān}), with the respectful ending from two lessons back.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{খাওয়া}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{খাদ্}} (\emph{√khād}, \textquotedblleft{}to chew, to bite\textquotedblright{}), smoothed through Prakrit \emph{khā-}. Every neighbour eats with it: Hindi \emph{khānā}, Marathi \emph{khāṇe}, Gujarati \emph{khāvũ}, Punjabi \emph{khāṇā}.

Past Sanskrit the trail goes cold. \emph{Khād-} has no secure Indo-European pedigree outside Indo-Aryan, so there is no English cousin here — and one will not be manufactured. Some roots are simply local, and saying so is part of the method.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\bn{খ}} is \emph{kh}: a \emph{k} with a puff of breath behind it. Its plain partner \textbf{\bn{ক}} (\emph{k}) is the letter in Chapter 5's \emph{kāj}. The puff is not decoration — it is the whole difference between two words, and Bengali gives each its own letter.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Bengali eats its drinks}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
\bn{জল} \bn{খাওয়া} (\emph{jôl khāwā}) & to drink water — \textquotedblleft{}water-eat\textquotedblright{} \\
\bn{চা} \bn{খাওয়া} (\emph{chā khāwā}) & to drink tea \\
\bn{ওষুধ} \bn{খাওয়া} (\emph{oshudh khāwā}) & to take medicine \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Hindi keeps a second verb, \emph{pīnā}, for drinking. Bengali's everyday speech does not bother: whatever goes in the mouth is \emph{khāwā}. There \textbf{is} a drink-verb — \bn{পান} \bn{করা} (\emph{pān kôrā}), noun-plus-\emph{kôrā} in exactly Chapter 5's \emph{kāj kôrā} shape, built on Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{পা}} (\emph{√pā}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{}), whose Latin cousin \emph{pōtāre} gives English \textbf{potion} and \textbf{potable}. But it belongs to writing and ceremony. Ask for tea in a Kolkata kitchen and you eat it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}khāwā\textquotedblright{} — eat — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi khāi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the drinking Bengali eats — \textquotedblleft{}jôl khāwā … chā khāwā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the formal drink-verb and its English cousins — \textquotedblleft{}pān kôrā … potion, potable\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}drink water\textquotedblright{} in everyday Bengali? (\textbf{\bn{জল} \bn{খাওয়া}} — literally \textquotedblleft{}water-eat.\textquotedblright{}) Which Sanskrit root is \emph{khāwā}, and does English share it? (\textbf{√khād}, \textquotedblleft{}to chew\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{no}, the root goes no further than Indo-Aryan.) Which verb would a formal text use for drinking, and what English words does its root reach? (\textbf{\bn{পান} \bn{করা}}, from \emph{√pā} — English \emph{potion}, \emph{potable}.) Next: one spelling, two vowels.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dækhā]{\bn{দেখা} (dækhā) — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} and a vowel that moves under a fixed spelling}

\label{lesson:BN-C07-dekha}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 4 buried this verb inside \emph{dækhā hôbe}, \textquotedblleft{}a seeing will happen.\textquotedblright{} Prised out on its own, it carries a sound rule that runs through every verb in this chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{দেখা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দেখা}} — \emph{dækhā} — \textbf{to see, to look}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{দেখি} (\emph{āmi dekhi}), \textquotedblleft{}I see.\textquotedblright{} \bn{সে} \bn{দেখে} (\emph{se dækhe}), \textquotedblleft{}he sees.\textquotedblright{} Read those two romanizations again — they are not the same vowel.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{দেখা}} is traced to Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{দৃশ্}} (\emph{√dṛś}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}) through the Prakrit stem \emph{dekkha-}; Hindi's \emph{dekhnā} is the same word. Sanskrit built \emph{darśana}, \textquotedblleft{}a viewing,\textquotedblright{} on that root, and further back it is PIE \emph{*der\'{k}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to see clearly.\textquotedblright{} Greek took it for \emph{dérkomai}, \textquotedblleft{}I look,\textquotedblright{} and for \emph{drákōn}, the sharp-gazing serpent — which English borrowed as \textbf{dragon}. Bengali's \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} and England's dragons are one word, wearing very different clothes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\bn{দ}} is a soft dental \emph{d}, tongue on the teeth. The vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ে}} on it is written identically every time — but Bengali says it either as a close \emph{e} (as in English \emph{bay}) or an open \emph{æ} (as in English \emph{bat}), and the page will never tell you which.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending decides the vowel}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\bn{আমি} \bn{দেখি} & \emph{dekhi} — close \emph{e} \\
\bn{সে} \bn{দেখে} & \emph{dækhe} — open \emph{æ} \\
\bn{তুমি} \bn{দেখো} & \emph{dækho} — open \emph{æ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The rule: when the ending carries the high vowel \emph{-i}, the stem vowel closes to \emph{e}. Any other ending leaves it open at \emph{æ}. That is \textbf{vowel harmony}, and the verb of the first lesson does it too — \bn{আমি} \bn{হই} (\emph{hôi}, closed) against \bn{সে} \bn{হয়} (\emph{hôy}, open). It is a rule your ear must carry alone, because the spelling never budges.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dækhā\textquotedblright{} — then the pair, \textquotedblleft{}dekhi … dækhe\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same shift on the be-verb — \textquotedblleft{}hôi … hôy\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root and its odd English relative — \textquotedblleft{}dṛś … dragon\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending closes the stem vowel to \emph{e}? (\textbf{The \emph{-i} of \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{dekhi}, against \emph{dækhe} and \emph{dækho}.) Does the spelling record that? (\textbf{No} — \bn{দে} is written the same either way; only the ear knows.) Which English animal shares this verb's root? (\textbf{The dragon} — Greek \emph{drákōn}, from PIE \emph{*der\'{k}-}.) Next: the last verb, and the knowing English lost.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jānā]{\bn{জানা} (jānā) — \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} and the knowing English gave up}

\label{lesson:BN-C07-jana}



\begin{quote}
Six thousand years ago this verb and the English word you are reading it with were the same word. They still are. But Bengali kept a distinction English threw away.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{জানা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জানা}} — \emph{jānā} — \textbf{to know}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{জানি} (\emph{āmi jāni}), \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{} \bn{আপনি} \bn{জানেন} (\emph{āpni jānen}), respectfully.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{জানা}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{জ্ঞা}} (\emph{√jñā}, \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{}), the root under \emph{jñāna}, \textquotedblleft{}knowledge.\textquotedblright{} Behind it stands PIE \emph{*ǵneh\textsubscript{3}-}, and English is full of its children: \textbf{know} and \textbf{knowledge} by the direct Germanic road; \textbf{notice}, \textbf{recognize} and \textbf{cognition} through Latin \emph{nōscere}; \textbf{gnosis} and \textbf{diagnosis} through Greek \emph{gign\'{\={o}}skein}. Bengali \emph{jāni} and English \emph{know} are one verb, separated only by time.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
Sanskrit writes the root with \textbf{\bn{জ্ঞ}}, a knot of \emph{j} and \emph{ñ}. Bengali does not say \emph{jñ} at all — it says \textbf{gg}, so \emph{jñāna} comes out \emph{ggān}. The plain verb spares you the knot: \textbf{\bn{জানা}} is simply \bn{জা} + \bn{না}, \emph{jā-nā}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two knowings, and English has one word for both}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{what it knows} \\
\midrule
\bn{জানা} (\emph{jānā}) & a fact, or how to do something \\
\bn{চেনা} (\emph{chenā}) & a person or a place, by acquaintance \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\bn{আমি} \bn{জানি} — \textquotedblleft{}I know\textquotedblright{} (that it is so). \bn{আমি} \bn{তাকে} \bn{চিনি} (\emph{āmi tāke chini}) — \textquotedblleft{}I know him,\textquotedblright{} meaning I am acquainted with him. Say \emph{jāni} of a person and you have said you know facts about them, which is a colder thing.

English once had this line and lost it; French still walks it as \emph{savoir} against \emph{connaître}, German as \emph{wissen} against \emph{kennen}, Spanish as \emph{saber} against \emph{conocer}. And listen to \emph{chini} beside \bn{সে} \bn{চেনে} (\emph{se chæne}): the same vowel harmony as the last lesson, on a brand-new verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}jānā\textquotedblright{} — know — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi jāni\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other knowing — \textquotedblleft{}āmi tāke chini\textquotedblright{}
  \item the harmony again — \textquotedblleft{}chini … chæne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the six verbs of this chapter — \textquotedblleft{}hôwā, jāwā, āsā, khāwā, dækhā, jānā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb knows a person, and which knows a fact? (\textbf{\bn{চেনা}} for people, \textbf{\bn{জানা}} for facts — the \emph{connaître} / \emph{savoir} line.) Name three English children of this root. (\textbf{Know}, \textbf{notice}, \textbf{diagnosis} — Germanic, Latin, Greek.) Why does \emph{chini} close its vowel where \emph{chæne} keeps it open? (\textbf{Vowel harmony} — the \emph{-i} ending closes the stem vowel, as in \emph{dekhi}.) That closes the chapter: six verbs, no gender on any of them, and the respect always sitting in the ending.
\end{tcolorbox}
